accuracy.evidence: Research claims are kept to what the studies found: Emmons and McCullough (2003) weekly gratitude lists and Froh, Sefick and Emmons (2008) counting blessings with early adolescents both reported modest gains in well-being, so the lesson says 'a little better', 'small but real', and 'not a cure'. Curriculum links checked against the PSHE Association KS2 programme (feelings and mental health strategies), DfE Relationships and Health Education 2019, and NHS Five Ways to Wellbeing ('take notice'). The 3 x 7 = 21 and 12 + n items were checked at the range corners.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the known problems with teaching gratitude to children: only big things count (size prediction, challenge 'big'), using gratitude to dismiss sadness, the 'toxic positivity' slip (sad-and-glad scene options 'fake' and 'ban', mastery m2 hamster item), seeing good things as just appearing with no person behind them (who prediction, 'nobody'), and vague automatic thanks (note scene and sorter).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagglad's mechanism is gratitude itself: a jar that only accepts good moments from a mixed day while refusing to call a grazed knee good, linking people to the good things they caused, holding a sad scenario next to a good thing, and assembling a thank-you note from what-they-did and how-it-helped parts with vague parts rejected. No other flagship builds a note or matches benefactors; the distinctness gate measured it under 30% against all labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds three good things in a day that also had rain, a lost pencil and a graze, so they discover that a bad day still has good bits; the who scene ends by revealing farmers and a shop behind the lunch; sorting shows small things outnumber big ones; picking among sad-and-glad answers shows that honest feelings and gratitude coexist; the note builder rejects 'Thanks for everything' until the note is specific.

predictions.evidence: The who prediction offers 'Nobody, it was just there', a common child view, which the matching scene then disproves by giving every good thing a person. The size prediction offers 'only big things count', and the sort shows three everyday small good things that go in the same jar.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven why() messages name the slip: only big things count (big), pretending to be happy (fake), seeing nothing good (none), good things just appear (nobody), vague thanks (vague), thankful people cannot be sad (ban), and the 3 x 7 count error (sum).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and concrete examples a 9 year old knows (warm socks, a friend's smile, column adding). Canvas cards were shortened to two or three words after the 360 px check (Help with sums, Leo let me play). The adult text was rewritten into shorter sentences after validate_lessons.py flagged grade 11.4; it now passes the limit.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph teaches one part of the habit: notice big and small, notice the person, do not pretend, be specific. The adult text gives curriculum, what the research does and does not show, named mistakes and the lab tasks; the content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with the please-and-thank-you lesson and all others.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px light and dark screenshots after each Show me and mid-demo: the day uses two rows of four 77 px cards with captions of at most three lines, the who scene uses two full-height columns of 60 px rows, the sad-and-glad and note options are full-width rows, and the note text wraps inside the card. Every action is also a full-width button under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Buttons cover every move: each moment to the jar, each person to the next unmatched good thing, each item to Big or Small, each sad-and-glad answer, and each note part. Every move updates the canvas aria-label and live region with the full sentence (for example the finished note). walk.cjs ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no violations; text is dark ink on white or pale cards.
